pages.text: How to Eat Your Way Through Penang, Malaysia's Island of Hawker Stalls and Street Art | National Geographic TRAVEL BEST OF THE WORLD Find Out Why Penang Is Asia’s Most Exciting Emerging Region Anchored by the historic city of George Town, the Malaysian state is a melting pot of influences in one of the most picturesque places on the planet. Traditional Chinese lanterns hang in front of the Acheen Street Mosque in George Town, the capital city of Penang. Chris Schalkx, Kintzing By Kristin Braswell Published October 20, 2026 Separated by a narrow strip of sea, the Malaysian state of Penang has dual personalities: On Penang Island, travelers can explore the historic streets of George Town, the capital city, before heading to rainforest-fringed beaches. On the mainland Seberang Perai, across the Penang Strait, traditional villages and winding mangrove rivers sit alongside industrial hubs. Chinese, Indian, Burmese, Arab, and European immigrants have shaped the cuisine, architecture, and religious identity of Penang, which was once a key trading post linking the Pacific and Indian Oceans. In George Town today, luxury hotels are housed in former Chinese merchant family estates, well-preserved colonial buildings, and narrow alleyways lined with murals and street food hawkers, giving the city a metropolitan pulse. In 2027, George Town's Penang Hill Cable Car will begin gliding from the Penang Botanic Gardens to the top of Penang Hill in less than 10 minutes, revealing panoramic vistas of rainforest canopies. pages.text: How to Experience Iceland's Fire and Ice in Reykjavík | National Geographic TRAVEL How to Experience Iceland's Fire and Ice in Reykjavík Iceland’s capital lives up to the country’s nickname — the Land of Fire and Ice — with geologically rooted cultural curiosities, bathing pools, bars and restaurants The design of Hallgrímskirkja, Reykjavík’s main church, is said to have been inspired by the country’s mountains. Getty By Daniel Stables Published October 22, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). The world’s northernmost capital, Reykjavík is a culturally vibrant city, home to around one third of Iceland’s population. Yet, it still feels close to the duelling forces of nature that define the country’s life and landscape: glaciers and snow-capped mountains above ground; and an infernal volcanism seething below the surface, heating geothermal pools and hot springs. Clues to this unique dynamic are everywhere in Reykjavík. It runs almost exclusively on geothermal power — the only capital city in the world to do so. The tap water, naturally filtered through mazes of volcanic rock, is preternaturally pure and good for the skin (you’ll soon get used to the slightly eggy, sulphurous smell). Galleries host displays of artwork hewn from glacier ice, while immersive exhibits take you deep into the belly of the Earth. Some of the country’s most spectacular bathing pools are found right here, too, ensuring your time in Reykjavík will be, quite literally, immersive. pages.title: How to Experience St Moritz’s Snow Polo World Cup Weekend | National Geographic
pages.description: Polo ponies, palace hotels and oysters on ice: the Snow Polo World Cup St Moritz returns every January for two days of high-altitude glamour. Here’s how to make the most of it.
pages.text: How to Experience St Moritz’s Snow Polo World Cup Weekend | National Geographic By Emma Al-Mousawi Published November 14, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). For one weekend in late January, frozen Lake St Moritz, encircled by Switzerland’s snow-heaped Engadin Alps, becomes the glittering stage for one of polo’s most prestigious events: the Snow Polo World Cup St Moritz. Sunglass-clad spectators in cashmere, elegant coats and designer puffer jackets gather as champagne flutes clink and oysters are shucked. On the ice, six teams of white-slacked players thunder across the 200-metre pitch, competing for the coveted trophy against the dazzling backdrop of one of Europe’s oldest and most exclusive ski resorts. Polo traces its origins back more than two millennia to the grasslands of Persia, but its snowy incarnation is decidedly younger. It was conceived here just over 40 years ago by Reto Gaudenzi, a local player and founder of Switzerland’s first polo team. Undeterred by the fact that polo had never been played on snow, he experimented with hoof grips and a larger, slower orange ball. A successful trial followed in 1984; a year later, the world’s first snow polo tournament was staged on the lake before more than 1,000 spectators. Today, the three-day event draws crowds of 26,000 — and dozens of private jets. Forty grooms tend 120 ponies in heated stables, while three daily matches unfold on snow-covered ice at least 50cm thick. pages.title: How to Explore the Indian Ocean Through Its Spices | National Geographic
pages.description: Once among the world’s most valuable commodities, spices transformed the Indian Ocean, enriching empires while weaving together the cultures, cuisines and communities of distant shores. Today, travellers can still follow those ancient routes through fragrant plantation visits, cooking classes and market tours.
pages.text: How to Explore the Indian Ocean Through Its Spices | National Geographic By Daniel Stables Published September 19, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Nowadays, most of us take spices for granted — a pinch of cinnamon in porridge, black pepper over pasta or cumin stirred into a curry. Yet for centuries these everyday ingredients shaped the course of history. The trade in black pepper facilitated cultural and economic intermixing between ancient Rome and India, while camels pulled frankincense caravans across the deserts that separated Africa and Asia, taking with them ideas, recipes, music and language. Today, these influences can still be felt in many countries, offering a fascinating, and often delicious, theme through which to explore a place. Browse the Spice Souks of Muscat, Oman Located on the Arabian Sea between Saudi Arabia, Yemen and the UAE, the seafaring nation of Oman has long been a link between East Africa, India and Southeast Asia. That story is told in the spice section of Muttrah Souk, the Omani capital’s historic covered market, where technicolour cones of powdered ginger, turmeric and cumin sit alongside piles of frankincense rocks, bundled strands of saffron, and less familiar items like loomi — black, sun-dried limes. The air hangs particularly heavy with the scent of frankincense, which Omanis use to perfume their homes, cars and traditional robes. pages.text: How to Explore the Pantanal | National Geographic A school of fish and a hungry caiman in the waters of the Pantanal region Photograph by Luciano Candisani, National Geographic TRAVEL How to Explore the Pantanal Explore the Pantanal from all corners with this guide to the beauty of this national park and UNESCO World Heritage site. By Avery Stonich Published August 4, 2016 • 4 min read The Pantanal is the world’s largest wetland , pooling over 81,000 square miles (210,000 square kilometers)—an area nearly the size of Kansas—in the center of South America, mostly in central-western Brazil and straddling the borders of Paraguay and Bolivia. Often overshadowed by the Amazon to the north, the Pantanal quietly harbors the highest concentration of wildlife in South America . It’s part national park and part UNESCO World Heritage site , and it’s considered a critical region of the world by the World Wildlife Fund, which estimates that 325 species of fish, 159 species of mammals, 656 species of birds, 53 species of amphibians, and 98 species of reptiles live in this hotbed of biodiversity. Cattle in the marshlands of the Nhecolandia region, Mato Grosso do Sul, Brazil Photograph by Yann Arthus-Bertrand, Getty Images If You Go The Pantanal teems with life in every season. The dry season, July to October, is the best time to see mind-boggling concentrations of wildlife clustered around water holes. pages.text: How to explore the tropical side of Japan in Okinawa | National Geographic TRAVEL How to explore the tropical side of Japan in Okinawa With its laid-back seafaring culture and unique wildlife, the Yaeyama archipelago in Japan’s far southern Okinawa prefecture reveals a different side to Japan. The traditional Okinawan sabani boats were historically used for fishing and travelling between islands. Photograph by James Whitlow Delano By Georgia Stephens Published January 7, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). It’s show time. Up heaves the sail, a concertina of heavy canvas pulled taut against the creaking wooden mast. It gulps the breeze that’s whisking cotton puffs of cloud out to sea. Black butterflies, big as sparrows, rise from the steep jungle at our backs as the droning of cicadas meets the surf raking the beach. The air is flower-scented, hot and heavy as water. Up comes the anchor, out come the paddles; the nose of the traditional sabani boat plunges into the waves. Any sailor leaving Ishigaki island needs to be absolutely certain of their course. Head north west, and the next landfall lies hundreds of miles away in China; east, and it’ll be the considerably farther-flung shores of Mexico. Here, in southern Okinawa Prefecture, Japan fizzles out in a spray of its remotest isles. Closer to Taiwan and the Philippines than the mainland and fed by warmer currents, the subtropical Yaeyama Islands, of which Ishigaki is a part, are unique within Japan. How many of them are true is another matter, but there's no denying the strange pull of the chilling spots where many of them took place. pages.text: How To Find Dinosaur Bones | National Geographic TRAVEL DIGITAL NOMAD How To Find Dinosaur Bones By Andrew Evans Published July 29, 2013 • 7 min read Though I travel far and wide, it is rare that I get to travel so far back in time (to the Cretaceous period) and walk among the gigantic wildlife (dinosaurs) who once romped along the tropical shores of central Montana . Admittedly, I was once a young boy with a bedroom full of plastic dinosaurs and an obsession with beasts for which there was no zoo, and traveling to Montana turned me back into that very same kid, giddy with the thrill of hunting down any vague remnant of the prehistoric past. Now, finding dinosaur bones is hard work , and not as simple or quick as the movies might indicate, but just an hour after heading out from the Two Medicine Dinosaur Center , I had already spotted and correctly identified my first real dinosaur bone fragment. I spent the rest of the day digging in the dirt, imagining the Hadrosaurid and Ceratopsian melee that took place on this very spot. One day on a dig does not a paleontologist make, but in the time I spent searching for dinosaurs, I sure learned a lot—like how I lack the patience it takes to be a paleontologist but how awesome it would be. I also learned the seven fundamental steps behind finding dinosaur bones: 1. Where and when to go When it comes to wildlife safaris, Africa is unrivalled in terms of its variety. But the tail end of the wet season is less crowded and arguably just as spectacular, with the bonus of dramatic skies and verdant grasslands. If you suspect someone stole your personal information or identity, placing a credit freeze can help protect you from fraud. What is a credit freeze? When you place a security freeze , creditors cannot access your credit report. This will keep them from approving any new credit account in your name, whether it is fraudulent or legitimate. To let lenders and other companies access your credit files again to create new accounts, you will need to lift your credit freeze permanently or temporarily. Place or lift a credit freeze Freeze or lift the freeze on your credit report for free by contacting each of the three major credit reporting agencies: Equifax Experian TransUnion You can submit your request online, by phone, or by mail. Annexed by an endless parade of empires — including the Greeks, Romans, Byzantines and Ottomans — in 1878, Cyprus became a British protectorate. These last rulers chose the lofty, leafy Troodos Mountains as their summer capital to escape the heat of the coast, and it’s still favoured by locals from spring to autumn. Cyprus became independent in 1960, but vestiges of its storied past are everywhere, from its ancestral grapes, mavro and xynisteri, to mural-washed churches hidden among the hills and turn-of-the-century mansions left by long-gone grandees. Scattered as if on a pirate’s map off England’s southwesterly tip, the Isles of Scilly aren’t a place you stumble over. Travellers need to have booked well ahead for the short, spectacularly scenic transfer by twin-prop plane or helicopter from Penzance to the 140-strong archipelago. Or embark on a three-hour, dolphin-flanked ferry, which plies azure waters towards show-off shelves of pristine white sand. It’s a pilgrimage richly rewarded by a landscape of palms, lipstick-pink sea thrift and sky-blue agapanthus flowers, framing sand-blown, barely-there roads. Beyond St Mary’s, the largest and most populous isle, there are few cars on the four other inhabited outposts of Tresco, Bryher, St Martin’s and St Agnes. They offer a daily invitation to hike and island-hop, with dockings dictated by the tides, and crossings taking mere minutes on jetboat ferries with names like Firethorn and Thunder. From its mountainous national parks to its scenic rail journeys, Norway has so many highlights, it’s hard to know how to begin planning an itinerary. Knowing how to get around and how best to make the most of your money are two essentials for unlocking all the country has to offer — read on to discover these and more tips for creating your perfect trip. pages.text: How to plan the ultimate road trip through Tasmania | National Geographic By Justin Meneguzzi Published June 19, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). Home to the Aboriginal Palawa people for 40,000 years, Tasmania was settled by Europeans from 1803. They found a maritime climate, volcanic soils and some of the cleanest air in the world. These bountiful conditions have since helped the apple-shaped island build its reputation for producing superlative wine, whisky and cheese. On a road trip across Australia’s smallest state, preserved colonial-era towns and farms seem to appear around every corner, while mountains and valleys knitted together by walking trails provide chances to stretch your legs. Meanwhile, after centuries of oppression, the Palawa people invite visitors to connect with their ancestral homelands through the sights, sounds and flavours of the bush. You could easily drive coast to coast in six hours, but why rush? Tasmanians know that having patience and adopting a slower pace are key to enjoying the finer things in life. Plan up to a week for a road trip from the coast to the high country, starting in the historic southeastern port city of Hobart, Tasmania’s state capital, and finishing in the northerly hub of Launceston. Palm-fringed surf bays, tea plantation hikes, ancient ruins and incense-filled temples — few islands can match the diversity of Sri Lanka. First-timers tend to head south for beach-hopping and safaris, but the developing north offers an equally rich experience, along with an insight into the island’s Tamil culture. Here are two handpicked itineraries that show off the best of both sides of the island. Highlights of the South A classic circuit of the country’s southern half takes in highland tea plantations, Buddhist pilgrimage sites and heritage towns — as well as some of its finest surf hubs. 1. Kandy Best For: Temple Pilgrimages The last stronghold in Sri Lanka to fall to the British in 1818, Kandy was once a royal seat and remains an important cultural and religious centre. Enthroned in the lush highlands, the city has a large lake at its heart, with royal bathhouse ruins, tiny bee-eaters in the trees and vendors selling chilli-mango at its edges. Pilgrims come from all over the Buddhist world to attend the thrice-daily puja (worship) ceremony at the Temple of the Tooth, a bone-white complex that holds a relic of Buddha himself, protected by bristling walls of elephant tusks. Thanks to its northern latitude and clear night skies, Edmonton is a prime spot to view the auroras. Explore Edmonton By Brendan Sainsbury Published May 12, 2026 Nature’s most spectacular light show, the Aurora Borealis, will be even more dazzling this year. This is thanks to a phenomenon called the ‘solar maximum’, defined as the ‘peak’ of the sun’s activity over its 11-year cycle. One of the best places to take advantage of this astronomical event is in Edmonton — North America’s most northerly city, set at latitude of 53.5ºN. With a landscape of wide-open plains, Edmonton and the surrounding region offers a front-row seat to the wonders of the galaxy. Here’s how to spot the auroras using Alberta’s capital as your base. When should I go? Though the solar maximum technically occurred in 2024, this high period of solar activity is expected to continue well into 2026. Put simply, this means that the sun will be sending more electrically charged particles to Earth than usual. These then convert to green, red, purple and blue light when they collide with our atmosphere, which we see as the auroras. Drawing visitors since the 1700s, North Norfolk has long been a place of escapism. You arrive ready to fill your lungs with sea air and let your gaze drift to the horizon. The natural beauty here is not the kind that smacks you in the face and overwhelms with superlatives. The expansive beaches, endless skies, fenland and watery network of the Broads are a more subtle tonic for the soul — you don’t have to work too hard to forget life beyond this somewhat overlooked patch of East Anglia. It’s also a place to get closer to wildlife. Many of the salt marshes in Norfolk offer some of Britain’s best birdwatching, while seals love to sunbathe on the shingle spits at Blakeney Point. Plus, there’s bluebell and snowbell carpets in spring, dragonflies buzzing over lavender fields in summer and woodland ablaze in ochre, yellow and red in autumn. Beyond the pull of its natural attractions, North Norfolk is dotted with stately homes, sliced through by heritage railways and framed by historic towns. Add it all together and you have a region that promises the kind of serenity many search far and wide for, yet few expect to find so close to home. pages.text: How to Spot the ‘Loneliest Star’ in the Autumn Night Sky | National Geographic SCIENCE NIGHT SKY GUIDE How to Spot the ‘Loneliest Star’ in the Autumn Night Sky Just 25 light-years from Earth, Fomalhaut is surrounded by vast belts of dust that could reveal the gravitational fingerprints of undiscovered worlds. Fomalhaut, one of the brightest stars in the autumn night sky, lies about 25 light-years from Earth. Roughly 15 times as luminous as our sun, the star is surrounded by vast belts of dust that may hold clues to planets astronomers have yet to discover. NASA, ESA, and the Digitized Sky Survey 2 By Stefanie Waldek Published October 23, 2026 On an autumn night in the Northern Hemisphere, Fomalhaut appears as a bright pinprick in a field of darkness, far from other bright stars. But the star’s apparent solitude is only part of its story: It sits at the center of an expansive system of dusty belts that may hold clues to worlds we have yet to find. Fomalhaut’s name comes from the Arabic fam al-ḥūt , meaning “mouth of the fish,” reflecting its place in the constellation Piscis Austrinus, or the Southern Fish. In a tradition attributed to ancient Persia, Fomalhaut is one of four “Royal Stars,” celestial markers associated with the cardinal directions. The agency drafts its own documents, called guidances, that provide the FDA’s current thinking on how best to comply with laws and regulations governing food, feed and other FDA-regulated products. But food industry associations also draft guidance documents to capture the best practices to produce food, feed and other regulated products in a way that meets federal safety standards. For example, food industry associations may want to draft guidance documents to help their members comply with new requirements under the FDA Food Safety Modernization Act (FSMA). Max Emanuelson By Ally Wybrew Published November 17, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). “We call that the smell of money,” grins Tamara Singer, in response to my scrunched-up nostrils. I’m picking my way down the rocky shores of the remote Lofoten archipelago in Norway’s Arctic Circle, trusting my footing to the woolly-hat-wearing, wetsuit-clad co-founders of Lofoten Seaweed, Tamara and Angelita Eriksen. As we walk, I can’t take my eyes off the macabre scene: hundreds of stockfish hang from the hjells (wooden trellises) lining the road while row upon row of empty racks stand between them. I ask how many fish are hanging here. “There used to be a lot more,” Tamara says, her response subdued. The large gaps in the racks speak volumes about the state of an industry that was once the economic backbone of the country. The move not only restricts the export of advanced chips, but also access to their computing power, which Chinese firms currently rent abroad to train artificial intelligence (AI) models. South East Asian countries in particular have invested heavily in data centres to power their AI ambitions - and Chinese firms seeking computing power overseas have been a key market. This allows Washington to monitor if those chips are being used to serve Chinese companies, or being smuggled to China. Stepping out, National Geographic Explorer Gina Moseley breathed deeply and took in the commanding view of Greenland ’s barren landscape. To the south, a frozen lake stretched out for miles, eventually giving way to brown and gray plateaus, interrupted by the white flash of glaciers in the distance. In the other direction, some 560 miles beyond the horizon, was the North Pole. The only other human presence was the helicopter pilot and the other passengers: Moseley’s life partner and this story’s photographer and fellow National Geographic Explorer, Robbie Shone, and technical climbing specialist Chris Blakeley. The weather was mild, just above freezing—perfect, actually—but Moseley knew that storms could blow up at a moment’s notice, bringing dangerous winds and dense fog. The Vienna Philharmonic Ball is held in the Golden Hall of the Musikverein. Paul Bauer, Wien Tourismus By Ellen Himelfarb Published October 12, 2026 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). On 11 November, Vienna’s palaces and music halls kick into high gear. Dance floors swarm with couples waltzing in choreographed swirls — and freestyling to live electropop. The two scenes are complementary halves of the Austrian capital’s modern ball scene: an old custom attracting new attention, buoyed by social media and miles of bias-cut silk. The festivities trace their roots to the 1700s, when Emperor Joseph II opened the Hofburg Palace dances — until then, reserved for nobility — to ordinary citizens. The decision paved the way for a wider ball culture to develop in the following centuries. Public dancing venues expanded, professional groups began holding their own balls and the dances became key fixtures in the city’s social calendar — a tradition that continues to this day. When Gen Z came of age, they box-stepped into Ballsaison (ball season) fuelled by a penchant for retro style and, crucially, posting the pageantry online. pages.text: How Wales captain Dewi Lake's rousing speech inspired historic win against All Blacks - BBC Sport Image source, Huw Evans Picture Agency Image caption, Dewi Lake has captained Wales 24 times Published 16 November 2026 Inside the Wales dressing room at the Principality Stadium at half-time on Saturday, heads could easily have bowed. Visitors New Zealand had just levelled the scores at 21-21 with the clock in the red at the end of the first half. It was a sucker punch that could have knocked the wind out of Welsh sails. But captain Dewi Lake summoned the words that inspired a first win over New Zealand in 73 years. With a rousing speech, the captain reminded his players of the feeling in the same changing room 12 months earlier, when they trailed by just three points at the break only to eventually lose 52-26. "Dewi made a very good point, the last time that we played them we had been in the contest, but let the dam break," Leicester and Wales wing Gabriel Hamer-Webb told the Rugby Union Weekly podcast. "They slipped through and we promised ourselves that we weren't going to let that happen again, that we had an opportunity to really do something special. "The heart the boys showed from then on, we wanted it more than they did. New Zealand were shocked and there was no way that we were going to let it slip." Help for Survey Participants How We Conduct Our Surveys In addition to conducting the decennial census count, the Census Bureau conducts various surveys that study households, businesses, schools, hospitals, and more. The Census Bureau will notify you in advance if you are in a survey, provide different ways to respond, and may follow up with you. We notify you if you are in a survey. The U.S. Census Bureau typically sends an official letter describing the survey for which your household or business has been selected and why your participation is important. This letter describes what the survey is, what type of questions will be asked, and what you can expect as a survey participant. For household surveys, most mailings from the Census Bureau are addressed to “the resident of.” Household surveys from the Census Bureau are only mailed to residential addresses, not to P.O. Boxes. P.O. Boxes are not associated with specific addresses, so the Census Bureau cannot use them as a mailing destination. If you are visited by a field representative working on a survey and have not yet received a survey letter or notice from the Census Bureau, you can request one from the representative at your door. You may also contact the Census Bureau Regional Office for your state for more information. Some surveys send invitations via text message or email. You can verify an email or text message is from the Census Bureau by noting the email address or phone number from which the invitation was sent.

August 20, 2024 HPV Vaccination Key points Protect your child from certain cancers later in life with HPV vaccine. CDC recommends 2 doses of HPV vaccine at ages 11–12 years. HPV vaccination can be started at age 9 years. Introduction HPV vaccination provides safe, effective, and lasting protection against the HPV infections that most commonly cause cancer. The HPV vaccine series is most effective when given before a person is exposed to the virus. Every year in the United States, HPV causes about 36,000 cases of cancer in both men and women. Keep Reading: Reasons to Get Vaccinated Available vaccines There are several types of HPV vaccines. That's why HPV vaccine is recommended earlier rather than later. It protects your child long before they ever have contact with the virus. Gardasil-9 Gardasil-9 (9vHPV) is the vaccine distributed in the United States. This vaccine protects against nine HPV types (6, 11, 16, 18, 31, 33, 45, 52, and 58). Other vaccine types In the past, the quadrivalent HPV vaccine (Gardasil, 4vHPV) and bivalent HPV vaccine (Cervarix, 2vHPV) were licensed by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). HPV Vaccine Recommendations For Health Care Providers July 9, 2024 Key points CDC recommends HPV vaccine for children 11 or 12 years old to protect against HPV infections that can cause some cancers later in life. HPV vaccination can be started at age 9 and is recommended through age 26 years for those who weren't vaccinated earlier. Introduction More than 15 years of data show that HPV vaccination provides safe, effective, and long-lasting protection against cancers caused by HPV infections. Research shows that healthcare professionals are parents’ most trusted source of information about the HPV vaccine. CDC encourages healthcare professionals to recommend HPV vaccination in the same way and on the same day that they recommend other vaccines for adolescents. This page summarizes CDC's current HPV vaccine recommendations. But after four years in the UK, the draw of home has proven too strong and they have returned to Ukraine's third largest city, undeterred by the sustained threat of air raids. "Friends of ours thought we were idiots for going back to Ukraine," reflects John, 74. "But returning is something we felt we needed to do. "Yes, it's dangerous. Yes, there are drones flying overhead. Yes, you can hear the explosions. But you just have to get on with life as best you can. "Home is Ukraine." During their time away, the pair sought sanctuary in Hull , East Yorkshire, where John was born and raised and has a property. He met Liliya, 64, in Ukraine and had been living there for 30 years until the invasion. "We had built a good life here," he says. pages.text: Human jaws are surprisingly strong and efficient | National Geographic SCIENCE NOT EXACTLY ROCKET SCIENCE Human jaws are surprisingly strong and efficient By Ed Yong Published June 22, 2010 • 4 min read Stephen Wroe has built a career out of analysing some of the planet’s most formidable skulls. His group at the University of New South Wales have studied the strength, sturdiness and biting power of the sabre-toothed cat , the great white shark , and the Komodo dragon . Now, he has turned his attention to a predator whose skull is far less impressive but yields surprises all the same – us. Humans, it is said, have relatively weak jaws that can’t inflict or withstand high bite forces. Some have suggested that we are adapted to eat foods that aren’t very tough, or that our use of tools and cooking has lessened the evolutionary pressure on maintaining sturdy jaws. Some have even suggested that our weedy jaw muscles made way for our large brains and thus facilitated their evolution. But according to Wroe, all of these explanations have a fatal flaw – our jaws aren’t weak at all. They’re actually remarkably efficient for a primate. The notion of weak human chops was based on very unrefined models that treated our jaws as two-dimensional levers. Of course, in real life, we chew in three glorious dimensions. To really understand how strong our mandibles are, we need to add that third dimension to the models. That’s exactly what Wroe did. He used his signature technique, called finite element analysis , to create a virtual model of a human skull (belonging to a San hunter-gatherer).

pages.text: Humans used to have straighter teeth—what changed? | National Geographic HEALTH Humans used to have straighter teeth—what changed? New research explores how diet, evolution, and facial anatomy may have shaped our modern smiles. Studies of ancient skulls show wider jaws and fewer malocclusions, leading researchers to explore how diet and lifestyle shaped the human face. Photograph by Alan/Adobe Stock By Leah Worthington Published July 15, 2025 Braces, rubber bands, even jaw surgery—millions endure them in pursuit of a straighter smile. But were misaligned smiles always this common? Research suggests that might not be the case. While malocclusions—crowded or misaligned teeth—have been found among our hunter-gatherer ancestors, they appear to be more prevalent in modern populations. So what changed? Experts say the answer isn’t simple but point to one possible culprit: our diets. As we traded raw, tough foods for softer, more processed ones, the burden of chewing decreased, allowing our jaws to shrink over time. Now, researchers are exploring how evolutionary biology, diet, and modern lifestyles may have reshaped our faces—and our smiles. How farming may have reshaped the human face Ancient human skulls were strikingly different from our own. Early hunter-gatherers had large, powerful jaws built for the demanding work of chewing tough meats, fibrous vegetables, seeds, and nuts. But around 12,000 years ago, things began to change. pages.text: Hundreds still homeless after 'unsafe' Canning Town flats evacuation Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Hundreds still homeless after being evacuated from 'unsafe' flats 4 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google Ayshea Buksh London BBC The Royal Gateway, also known as Caxton Works, was advertised as "an exciting regeneration project" when it was built Hundreds of residents in east London remain homeless after structural defects were discovered at an award-winning high-rise development that was declared "at risk of sudden collapse". The Royal Gateway, also known as Caxton Works in Canning Town, Newham, was built less than 10 years ago. But last month, people living there were suddenly told to leave - some in the middle of the night by London Fire Brigade - because it was "unsafe". Businesses renting commercial spaces were also told to evacuate their premises. Engineers identified concerns with reinforced concrete "transfer slabs" supporting the buildings - an issue that has emerged at other London developments, prompting wider scrutiny of the construction method. Property company Galliard Homes, which built the scheme, says it is working to "investigate the concerns and develop potential solutions", while giving financial and practical support to residents. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Hunting and Fishing The Bureau of Land Management provides opportunities to hunt, fish and engage in shooting sports activities in a safe and environmentally sound manner that promote marksmanship, public safety, hunter education, competition and lawful hunting. Over 99 percent of BLM-managed lands are open to hunting, fishing and recreational shooting opportunities. The BLM provides important access to hunting and fishing opportunities on public lands and waters, working with local communities and our valued partners to actively expand access to these opportunities. Find BLM Land near you. Online Interactive Map . Hunting America’s shared public lands provide habitat important for big, upland, and small game, furbearers and waterfowl and other game birds. The BLM manages 43 million acres of elk habitat, 131 million acres of mule deer habitat and 23 million acres of bighorn sheep habitat. BLM-managed lands are home to over 3,000 species , including big game, upland game birds and waterfowl.
